Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources

*Evidence briefing. Prepared for a working group on working-time policy.*

## Purpose

This briefing weighs five pieces of evidence on whether reducing the working week by a fifth, with pay maintained, raises productivity: the Halden multi-organisation pilot (source 1), the Varden County randomised trial at nine months (source 2), a re-analysis of the Halden pilot (source 3), a meta-analysis of 23 studies (source 4), and the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and of 14 Halden organisations (source 5). It adds no new data. Its aim is to state what the five together support, at the strength they support it, and what they leave open.

## 1. What each source contributes, and how later sources qualify it

**Source 1** established that many organisations that volunteered could cut scheduled hours by 20% with little change in reported output, and reported a 23.4% gain in output per hour, gains in every sector, large falls in sickness and resignations, and 92% continuation. Taken alone, it suggests a large, general effect.

**Source 2** was the first randomised evidence, with record-based output and actual hours. It introduced the distinction that the rest of the body depends on: between discretionary work, where output can be produced at any time within a deadline, and coverage-bound work, where output depends on presence while demand arrives. Per actual hour, output rose 12.5% in case-processing and 6.7% in counter work; per employee it was roughly unchanged in the first and fell 11.4% in the second. It also showed that actual hours fall less than scheduled hours, and that dividing by scheduled hours inflated the case-processing estimate from 12.5% to 22%.

**Source 3** found that source 1's figures were inflated in several documented ways: seven of nine withdrawals occurred after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons, not "during the preparation phase"; manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by 3.8 points; actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%; and the 1.4% revenue rise was a real fall of about 2.6% after inflation of 4.1%. Correcting what could be corrected reduced the per-hour gain to 10.8% in a subset. These findings stand. Source 3 then went further, concluding that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact, attributing the remainder to novelty on the basis of an extrapolated survey trend, and dismissing source 2's meetings hypothesis as post hoc. Those further claims do not survive later evidence.

**Source 4** placed both studies in a wider literature. Its pooled per-hour estimate of 13.4% is inflated by the same features source 3 identified; the estimates from controlled designs (+8.2%), actual-hours studies (+7.9%), record-based studies (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and bias adjustment (+9.1%) converge on roughly 8 to 10%. Its work-type moderator generalises source 2: per-worker output fell about 9% in coverage-bound settings, consistently, and was roughly maintained in discretionary ones. It rejected source 1's sector-general claim and source 3's artifact claim. Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong, for the reason source 5 gives.

**Source 5** applied the strictest standards in the body: randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and a two-year horizon. The per-hour gain in case-processing declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours) but remained clearly above zero. Output per employee stood at −3.4%, with a confidence interval including zero. A registered mediation test attributed 47% of the gain to fewer recurring meetings and 18% to reduced fatigue. Source 4's "no decay" conclusion rested on four long-follow-up studies, all uncontrolled and using scheduled hours. The counter arm was ended at month 12.

## 2. Weighing the estimates

**Table 1. Estimates of the change in output per hour, ordered by strength of design**

| Estimate | Source | Change per hour |
|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled, manager-reported, scheduled hours | 1 | +23.4% |
| Uncontrolled survivors, records, actual hours, 24 months | 5 | +11.8% |
| Uncontrolled subset, records, actual hours, 6 months | 3 | +10.8% |
| Meta-analysis, all studies | 4 | +13.4% |
| Meta-analysis, bias-adjusted | 4 | +9.1% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | 4 | +9.6% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 9 months, timesheets | 2 | +12.5% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 24 months, system logs | 5 | +8.5% |
| Randomised, counter work, 9 months | 2 | +6.7% |

Estimates fall as designs strengthen and stabilise around 8 to 10% for discretionary work. The figure of more than 20% is not supported by any design that measures actual hours.

## 3. What the body supports

Read as a whole, the five sources support a conditional answer.

1. **Per hour, yes, by a moderate amount.** In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours raises output per actual hour by roughly 8 to 10% under controlled measurement, with some decline from the first year to the second but no sign of disappearing within two years. The headline figure of more than 20% is an artifact of scheduled-hours denominators, manager-reported output and selection.
2. **Per worker, no.** Because actual hours fall by 11 to 14%, not 20%, a per-hour gain of 8 to 10% roughly offsets the hours cut but does not exceed it. Output per worker in discretionary work is around 2 to 4% lower than it would have been, with intervals that include zero. "Same output in four days" is close to true there; "more output" is not supported.
3. **In coverage-bound work, the answer is no on any measure that matters to the people served.** Output per worker falls by about 9 to 11%, waits lengthen, and maintaining service requires about 12% more staff. Per-hour gains exist but are small. This is the most consistent finding in the body.
4. **About half the per-hour gain in the best-measured setting comes from removing recurring meetings**, a smaller part from reduced fatigue, and about a third is unexplained.
5. **Sickness absence and resignations fall substantially** in every source that measured them (by roughly 27 to 36% for sick days). These are real benefits, but they are not themselves productivity, and the body does not estimate how far they offset per-worker output losses.

Whether "productivity" rises therefore depends on whether it is measured per hour or per worker, and on whether output in a given role depends on presence. Both slogans, "a four-day week makes people more productive" and "the gains are a mirage", are wrong as stated.

## 4. What the body leaves open

- **Is the hours cut necessary for the gain?** About half the per-hour gain runs through cutting meetings. Two control offices that audited meetings without cutting hours saw a 4.1% per-hour rise, but that is two offices without a comparison group. No study had an arm that reorganised work without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone would capture much of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and last, is not settled by this body.
- **Beyond two years.** No controlled evidence extends past 24 months. The per-hour gain declined between 9 and 24 months; whether it stabilises or continues to decline is unknown.
- **The unexplained third** of the per-hour gain has no tested mechanism.
- **Manufacturing and shift production** are almost absent from the evidence (two studies, both mixed).
- **Private-sector controlled evidence** is thin; the strongest designs are in public administration.

## 5. Bottom line

A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raises output per hour by roughly 8 to 10% in discretionary work, about half of it through fewer meetings, which roughly but not fully offsets the hours lost; in coverage-bound work it reduces output and service unless staff are added. Whether the gain requires the hours cut, or could be had by reorganising work alone, remains open.

response:
## What the briefing says

This is a policy synthesis of the five sources. It adds no new data. It traces how each later source qualified the earlier ones, then draws five conclusions:

1. Output per hour rises by roughly 8–10% in discretionary work under controlled measurement. There is some decline in year two, but no sign of the gain disappearing within two years.
2. Output per worker is about 2–4% lower, because actual hours fall 11–14%, not 20%.
3. Coverage-bound work loses about 9–11% of output, and waits lengthen.
4. About half the gain comes from cutting meetings.
5. Sickness absence and resignations fall.

It leaves open whether the hours cut is necessary for the gain, what happens beyond two years, the unexplained third of the gain, manufacturing, and private-sector settings. It rejects both popular slogans.

I checked every figure against the five source documents rather than against my earlier reviews. The briefing's conclusions are close to the ones I drew, so agreement alone isn't a check. The numbers are transcribed correctly throughout. The issues below are about the weight some claims are given, and about a few omissions that matter for a policy audience.

## Overall assessment

The briefing is faithful to its sources, and most of its claims are at the right strength:
- Per-hour and per-worker gains are kept separate.
- Coverage-bound work gets its own answer.
- The 20%+ figure is correctly attributed to scheduled-hours denominators, manager-reported output and selection.
- Section 4 lists the right open questions.

The main problem is in the Bottom line. It is the part the working group will quote, and it states two findings from one employer as general facts.

## Points to address

**1. The Bottom line generalises results from a single setting.**
- **Meetings share.** "About half of it through fewer meetings" comes from one mediation analysis in seven public-sector offices. Its interval is 28–66%. It rests on an assumption the authors themselves say a cluster trial can't guarantee, and it was tested on the same offices that generated the hypothesis. In the Bottom line it reads as a property of discretionary work in general. Point 4 in Section 3 does name "the best-measured setting," but the Bottom line drops that qualifier.
- **Staffing figure.** "About 12% more staff" in point 3 is the county's own estimate for its own counters. It is plausible elsewhere, but the evidence comes from one employer.

Suggested wording: *"…about 8 to 10% in discretionary work. In the one setting where it was tested, roughly half of this ran through fewer meetings…"*

**2. "Same output in four days" is misleading about time actually worked.**
Workers did not produce near-equal output in 32 hours. Across the sources, actual hours fell to about 33–35 a week, from longer remaining days, overtime and work on the day off. None of the Varden reports says whether staff worked four days or five shorter days. A more accurate summary: *"close to the same output with about 12% less time actually worked; the cut in scheduled time is not fully realised."* A working group designing a policy needs to know the scheduled cut does not translate one-for-one into time off.

**3. The sick-day figures have an unresolved problem.**
"Real benefits … roughly 27 to 36%" repeats figures that no source corrected for schedule type. If staff work four days, sick days counted in days fall about 20% with no change in the daily rate. That alone could reduce Halden's −36% to about −20%. The direction of the effect is probably real; the size is not established. The resignation figures carry further caveats:
- Halden: −56% among survivors, with no control group.
- Varden: 4.1% against 7.9% at 24 months, imprecise by the authors' own account.

"Substantially" should be qualified.

**4. The decline from nine to 24 months compares two different measures.**
Source 5's summary in Section 1 says 12.5% fell to 8.5%. The 12.5% is from timesheets and the 8.5% from system logs. On a like-for-like basis the change is 12.5% to 9.8%, about a fifth. The confidence intervals also overlap heavily, so "some decline" is correct, but the decline itself is not statistically established. Section 3, point 1 gets this roughly right; Section 1 should match.

**5. Some verdicts are stronger than the evidence.**
- "Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong": the evidence shows the claim was *unsupported*. Its four long-follow-up studies couldn't test for decay. The one controlled study suggests a modest decline, but not a statistically established one.
- "Those further claims [of source 3] do not survive later evidence": this is accurate for "entirely an artifact" and for the month-ten energy extrapolation. For the meetings dismissal, the registered test weakens source 3's objection but does not refute it. Its core complaint was that the finding wouldn't replicate, and no independent replication has been done.

**6. Table 1 is not ordered by strength of design, as its caption says.**
- The meta-analysis rows are pooled mixtures, not designs. They sit between uncontrolled studies and randomised ones.
- The counter-work row (+6.7%) is coverage-bound, while the text below the table draws a conclusion about discretionary work.
- The randomised nine-month estimate (+12.5%) is higher than two uncontrolled subsets (+10.8%, +11.8%). So "estimates fall as designs strengthen" is not monotonic. Follow-up length and the hours measure matter as well as design.

Splitting the table into discretionary and coverage-bound panels would fix most of this. Within each panel, order the rows by design and then by measure.

**7. Some things the working group needs are missing.**
- **Cost.** Discretionary offices paid about 3 hours a week of claimed overtime on top of full pay. Coverage-bound work needs more staff, and Varden estimated 9% higher cost per contact. The body contains no estimate of cost per unit of output. That is the question a working group will ask first, so it should be listed as open.
- **A reversion in discretionary work.** The briefing doesn't mention the Halden 24-month subset at all. Three of 14 organisations reverted, and one was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. That is a reversion in the category where the model is supposed to work. It is a single case, but relevant.
- **Classifying roles.** The policy recommendation depends on sorting roles into discretionary or coverage-bound. Most organisations have both. The meta-analysis flagged this, and the briefing should carry it forward, because it determines where any policy would apply.
- **Effects under evaluation.** The two-year gain was observed while staff knew they were being evaluated. Whether it holds as routine practice, without evaluation, is not the same question as whether it lasts beyond 24 months.
- **Replicating the mechanism.** The meetings result needs testing in new organisations, not only beyond two years in the same ones.

**8. A minor point on "convergence."**
The meta-analysis subgroups (controlled, actual hours, records, bias-adjusted) overlap heavily, so their agreement around 8–10% is not four independent confirmations. The 8–10% range still holds, because it is anchored by the Varden 24-month estimate of 8.5% (CI 3.4–13.8). But that interval is the honest statement of precision, and it is wider than "8 to 10%" suggests.

## Suggested Bottom line

> A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay reduces time actually worked by about 11–14%. In discretionary work, output per hour rises by roughly 8–10% (best estimate 8.5%, CI 3.4–13.8, at two years in one randomised trial), which nearly but not fully offsets the time lost: output per worker is about 2–4% lower, with intervals including zero. In the one setting where mechanisms were tested, roughly half the gain came from fewer recurring meetings. In coverage-bound work, output and service fall unless staff are added. Sickness absence and turnover appear to fall, though the size of the sickness effect is uncertain. Open: whether reorganisation without an hours cut would capture much of the gain; effects beyond two years and outside evaluation; costs per unit of output; and how to classify mixed roles.

I can produce a revised version of the full briefing with these changes made, marked so the working group can see each change and reverse it.
